blocks.text: The poem in verses 1–8 sets opposite experiences side by side—from birth and death to weeping and laughter—to portray the broad range of human life. It is descriptive rather than a sequence of commands: its point is not to approve every action named, but to show that life unfolds through changing and often uncontrollable times. The chapter then holds several realities together: God’s work endures beyond human comprehension; enjoyment of ordinary labor and food is presented as God’s gift; injustice can occupy places meant for justice; and death places humans alongside the animals in their shared mortality. These observations do not resolve every tension, but they frame human life as limited and changeable before God’s enduring action.

Verse 9 asks what lasting surplus or advantage a person can secure from labor. This makes the question more searching than whether work has immediate value: the chapter does commend rejoicing in one’s work, yet it also asks what enduring gain human effort can guarantee. The tension helps explain why the concluding enjoyment in verse 22 is called a person’s “portion,” rather than a claim to mastery over what comes afterward.
